title: Poor emotional regulation in anxious kids is linked to greater family accommodation ommodation/
author: Vladimir Hedrih
summary: This PsyPost summary of a study published in the Journal of Family Psychology examines why some families of anxious children fall more deeply into 'accommodation' — modifying routines, answering repetitive reassurance-seeking, or helping children avoid feared situations — than others. Drawing on baseline data from 90 children ages 7 to 17 with anxiety disorders or OCD, the researchers found that children with poorer emotional regulation experienced more family accommodation, and that the link between anxiety severity and accommodation was strongest specifically in children with low distress tolerance. In other words, it isn't anxiety alone that predicts how much a family bends around a child's fears; it's the child's capacity to tolerate distress that determines how much a family ends up accommodating. The study's practical takeaway, stated directly by the authors, is that interventions aimed at building a child's distress tolerance — rather than only managing anxiety symptoms or coaching parents to accommodate less — may be the more effective lever for reducing the accommodation cycle. The cross-sectional design means the study can show this pattern but not prove which direction the causation runs.
points: The finding that distress tolerance, not anxiety severity alone, is what most strongly predicts family accommodation redirects intervention focus from managing symptoms to building a specific skill: the ability to sit with discomfort.

Because the sample spans children with anxiety disorders and OCD specifically (a 'transdiagnostic' design), the accommodation-distress-tolerance link appears to hold across different anxiety presentations rather than being specific to one diagnosis.

The authors' own recommendation — 'Interventions targeting children's distress tolerance skills may help reduce family accommodation' — gives clinicians and parents a testable, actionable target rather than a vague call to 'accommodate less.'
quotes: The research examined 90 children (ages 7-17, average age 10) with anxiety disorders or OCD and their parents.

Results revealed that children with poor emotional regulation skills experienced greater 'family accommodation' — when parents modify their behavior to help children avoid anxiety-triggering situations.
Notably, the link between anxiety severity and family accommodation was strongest in children with low distress tolerance.
As the authors concluded: 'Interventions targeting children's distress tolerance skills may help reduce family accommodation among families of children with high levels of anxiety.'
Researchers analyzed baseline assessment data from a study comparing standard and bibliotherapy versions of the Supportive Parenting for Anxious Childhood Emotions (SPACE) program.
